title: Constrain plaintext collapse and test cyclic-column controls in Polygraphia III recovery
statement: An unknown-column attack groups artificial words by their last two characters, then maps those groups to letters by frequency or two coordinate-ascent sweeps on an external Latin bigram model. Across five Latin texts and three planted column sets each, held-out character accuracy averages 0.106–0.182 for the contextual search across 10, 24, and 131 random or cyclic columns; the known-column frequency oracle averages 0.162–0.362. The contextual output collapses to 3–7 distinct letters and improves held-out bigram loss in all 90 text/key/selection settings, showing that low loss alone is not adequate evidence of recovery.
check: Develop and compare a constrained unknown-column decoder that preserves a training-derived plaintext distribution and represents systematic word-form/column uncertainty. Fix the search budget, use disjoint books and held-out ciphertext, and test against independently specified iid and structured Markov or non-language controls. For cyclic selection, compare global shuffles with shuffles within known or independently inferred period-position strata; do not infer language or key recovery from a likelihood gain alone. Report letter and type accuracy against planted keys, detection calibration, alphabet collapse, multiple seeds, column collisions, unknown types and any disclosed key information.
method: Use Hermes P.III CSV at commit 0ef1439fa9d90aeab42951a51d0d5a0e27db1f8f; verify SHA-256 fe3f24a46dbc6b655eab8dbbd75addf84ee4a7dbd387ad802af75d02edfe5b4d. Test five pinned Latin books individually, excluding the entire target book from the external reference model; reference includes the remaining five pinned works, whose hashes are verified by the script. For each book, take its first 12,000 encipherable letters as ciphertext training and following 4,000 as test. Select 10, 24 or 131 table columns with seeds 41, 71, 103; choose uniformly at random or cycle sequentially. Decoder sees word strings only, the 24-letter candidate alphabet and external reference, but no plaintext, true mappings or column identity. Group each word by its last two characters; baseline matches groups sorted by frequency to reference letters sorted by frequency, with excess or unseen groups mapped to the commonest letter. Context search begins there and performs exactly two deterministic coordinate-ascent sweeps of all training groups, maximizing add-one smoothed reference bigram log likelihood; this allows multiple groups to map to the same letter. A same-cipher frequency search that receives true column IDs provides an intentionally stronger oracle benchmark. Accuracy is evaluated against the actual held-out characters, including ambiguous spellings; macro type accuracy averages each observed ciphertext spelling’s held-out correctness. Separately generate iid letters from the reference unigram distribution and first-order Markov sequences from its bigram distribution, then encipher them with the same seeded column selection. Shuffle held-out suffix groups 19 times either globally or within index modulo the selected column count, and compare test bigram loss using a lower-tail add-one p ≤ .05; the second null assumes knowledge of the selection period, not row identities.
findings: For cyclic columns, global shuffling detects a signal in 14/15 iid cases at 10 columns and 15/15 at 24, versus 0/15 under period matching for each. Under period matching the Markov controls are detected in 15/15 and 14/15, respectively. The comparison at 131 columns has only about 30 held-out tokens per period position and is particularly sparse. This shows that a global shuffle can mistake cyclic cipher structure for plaintext sequence dependence, while the stronger control still detects a non-semantic Markov process.
source: Jürgen Hermes, Polygraphia III: The cipher that pretends to be an artificial language, https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3313/paper7.pdf; table https://github.com/hermesj/R_Voynich_Stats/blob/0ef1439fa9d90aeab42951a51d0d5a0e27db1f8f/R%20code/Historical_ciphers/keys/ciphers_poly_III_in_order.csv

reproduce.instructions: Save script as /tmp/voy_piii_unknown.py and the pinned table as /tmp/voy-piii.csv. Fetch the project-pinned corpora with python3 -m vs fetch and run PYTHONPATH=. python3 /tmp/voy_piii_unknown.py from the repository root. It checks the table and reference-file SHA-256 values.

limitations: The five texts, not the 15 seed cases per cell, are the independent text units; the same 16,000-letter passage is reused across seeds. Two Bible books are related and the texts are not a representative medieval corpus. The search uses an observed suffix heuristic, candidate alphabet and a known language; it does not infer arbitrary column structures or prove that unknown-column recovery is impossible. The context model optimizes bigrams without marginal constraints and collapses output diversity. Nineteen permutations give only .05 resolution. The matched-period control knows the actual period and may itself have low power, particularly for 131 columns. The iid and Markov controls are diagnostic examples, not an exhaustive false-positive calibration. Nothing here evaluates or rules out a Voynich language–cipher cell.
